'''''Eucalyptus botryoides''''', commonly known as the '''bangalay''', '''bastard jarrah''', '''woollybutt'''<ref>{{cite book|title=Australian plants as Aboriginal Tools|author=Philip A. Clarke|publisher=Rosenberg Publishing|year=2012|isbn=978-1-922013-57-6}}</ref> or '''southern mahogany''', is a small to tall tree native to southeastern Australia. Reaching up to {{convert|40|m|ft|abbr=off}} high, it has rough bark on its trunk and branches. It is found on sandstone- or shale-based soils in open woodland, or on more sandy soils behind sand dunes. The white flowers appear in summer and autumn. It reproduces by resprouting from its woody [[lignotuber]] or epicormic buds after bushfire. ''E. botryoides'' hybridises with the Sydney blue gum (''[[Eucalyptus saligna|E. saligna]]'') in the Sydney region. The hard, durable wood has been used for panelling and flooring.

==Description==
In favourable conditions, ''Eucalyptus botryoides'' can grow as a straight-trunked tree to {{convert|40|m|ft|abbr=on}} high with a [[Diameter at breast height|dbh]] of {{convert|1|m|ft|abbr=on}}, although it is often shorter in poorer situations. In exposed areas behind sand dunes, it is a lower spreading tree {{convert|6|–|12|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall,<ref name="Boland">{{cite book|author1=Boland, Douglas J. |author2=Brooker, M. I. H. |author3=Chippendale, G. M. |author4=McDonald, Maurice William |title=Forest trees of Australia|publisher=CSIRO Publishing|location=Collingwood, Victoria|year=2006|pages=87–88|isbn=0-643-06969-0|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CRQg11hSJ1kC&q=%22Eucalyptus+botryoides%22+boland&pg=PA88}}</ref><ref name="Fuller">{{cite book|last1=Fuller|first1=Leon|title=Wollongong's Native Trees|date=1982|publisher=Weston & Co Publishers Pty Ltd|location=Kiama|isbn=0-9594711-1-1|pages=162–163|edition=Second}}</ref> with its leaves forming a dense [[Crown (botany)|crown]],<ref name=Fairley>{{cite book |author1=Fairley, Alan |author2=Moore, Philip |title=Native Plants of the Sydney District:An Identification Guide |year=2000 |edition= 2nd|publisher=Kangaroo Press |page=210|location=Kenthurst, NSW |isbn=0-7318-1031-7}}</ref> or even a multitrunked [[Mallee (habit)|mallee]] form in poor sandy soils.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Lacey | first1 = C. J. | title = Development of Large Plate-Like Lignotubers in ''Eucalyptus botryoides'' Sm. In Relation to Environmental Factors | doi = 10.1071/BT9830105 | journal = Australian Journal of Botany | volume = 31 | issue = 2 | pages = 105–18 | year = 1983 }}</ref> It has a swollen woody base known as a [[lignotuber]] which can reach {{convert|6|m|ft|abbr=on}} in diameter.<ref name=bm871>Benson and McDougall (1998), p. 871.</ref> The thick, fibrous, rough and flaky bark covers the trunk and larger branches, and is vertically furrowed.<ref name="floransw">{{NSW Flora Online|genus=Eucalyptus|species=botryoides |author=Hill, Ken}} Retrieved 19 January 2012.</ref> The bark is more greyish brown in trees of inland forest origin, and a redder brown in those of more coastal origin.<ref name="Boland"/> The bark on smaller branches is smooth and pale grey.<ref name=brooker/>

The adult leaves are stalked, broad-lanceolate, to {{convert|10|to|16|cm|in|abbr=on}} long by {{convert|2|–|6|cm|in|abbr=on}} wide, and are dark green above, and paler below.<ref name="floransw"/> Venation is fine and at 40° – 60° to the midline.<ref name="Fuller"/> Developing from small cylindrical or club-shaped (clavate) buds,<ref name="floransw"/> the white flowers appear from January to April,<ref name=Ben98/> and are arranged in groups of six to eleven in umbellasters. The woody fruits, or gumnuts, are ovoid or cylindrical in shape, and measure between 7–12 mm long and 4–6 mm wide, with the valve near the rim or enclosed.<ref name="floransw"/><!-- cites previous two sentences --><ref name="Fuller"/> Seedlings and young plants have more ovate leaves which are arranged oppositely along the stems for the first three to six pairs until they assume the adult alternately arranged configuration. They are also paler on the undersurface, and measure 4.5 to 11 cm long and 1.3 to 5.5 cm wide.<ref name="Boland"/><ref name="Fuller"/>

==Taxonomy==
The tree was first described by naturalist [[James Edward Smith (botanist)|James Edward Smith]] in 1797, without nominating a type specimen, and still bears its original name.<ref>Smith, J.E. (1797) Transactions of the Linnean Society of London 3: 286</ref><ref>{{APNI | name = ''Eucalyptus botryoides'' R.Br. | id = 4887}}</ref> The species name is derived from the [[Ancient Greek]] ''botrys'' "cluster", and may relate to the clustered flowerheads and fruit.<ref name="Boland"/> It has been classified in the subgenus ''Symphyomyrtus'', Section ''Latoangulatae'', Series ''Annulares'' (red mahoganies) by Brooker and Kleinig. Its closest relatives are the red mahogany (''[[Eucalyptus scias]]'') and the Blue Mountains mahogany (''[[Eucalyptus notabilis|E. notabilis]]''), red mahogany/red messmate (''[[Eucalyptus resinifera|E. resinifera]]'') and swamp mahogany (''[[Eucalyptus robusta|E. robusta]]'').<ref name=brooker>{{cite book|title=Field Guide to Eucalypts|volume=1: South-eastern Australia|author1=Brooker, M.I.H. |author2=Kleinig, D. A. |pages=73–78 |publisher= Bloomings Books|location= Melbourne |year= 1999|isbn=1-876473-03-7}}</ref> South of Sydney Harbour and Parramatta River, ''E. botryoides'' forms hybrid populations with Sydney blue gum (''[[Eucalyptus saligna|E. saligna]]'').<ref name=Ben98>{{cite journal|last=Benson |first=Doug |author2=McDougall, Lyn |year=1998 |title=Ecology of Sydney plant species:Part 6 Dicotyledon family Myrtaceae |journal=Cunninghamia |volume=5 |issue=4 |page=926 |url=http://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0008/58049/Cun5Ben808.pdf |archive-url=http://webarchive.loc.gov/all/20090614173442/http://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0008/58049/Cun5Ben808.pdf |archive-date=14 June 2009 |access-date=19 January 2012 }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Bangalay.JPG|thumb|Base of a large bangalay, [[Hacking River]], Australia]]
Distribution is coastal south eastern Australia from near [[Newcastle, New South Wales|Newcastle]] on the mid coast of [[New South Wales]] to eastern [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]] in the [[Lakes Entrance]] area, specifically [[Loch Sport, Victoria|Loch Sport]] south of [[Bairnsdale, Victoria|Bairnsdale]].<ref name=brooker/> The species was introduced to Western Australia, where it is listed as an [[alien (biology)|alien]].<ref>{{FloraBase|name=''Eucalyptus botryoides''|id=17359}}</ref> It grows predominantly on low nutrient sandstone-derived or sandy soils,<ref name=Ben98/> either behind coastal sand dunes or further inland in alluvial soils in valleys,<ref name="Boland"/> where it is a dominant tree. It is generally not far from salt water.<ref name=Fairley/><!-- cites previous 1.5 sentences --> ''Eucalyptus botryoides'' is only found in lowlands, from sea level to {{convert|300|m|ft|abbr=on}} altitude, and in areas of rainfall from {{convert|700|to|1300|mm|in|abbr=on}}.<ref name="Boland"/>

Trees in mixed open forest it grows with include turpentine (''[[Syncarpia glomulifera]]''), spotted gum (''[[Corymbia maculata]]''), red bloodwood (''[[Corymbia gummifera|C. gummifera]]''), blackbutt (''[[Eucalyptus pilularis|E. pilularis]]''), Sydney blue gum, red mahogany (''[[Eucalyptus resinifera|E. resinifera]]''),<ref name="Boland"/> and smooth-barked apple (''[[Angophora costata]]'').<ref name=Ben98/> Associated [[understory]] plants in wetter forests with some rainforest transition include lillypilly (''[[Syzygium smithii]]'') and [[Acacia|wattles]]. In coastal plant communities near sand-dunes, it grows with stunted forms of white stringybark (''[[Eucalyptus globoidea|E. globoidea]]''), silvertop ash (''[[Eucalyptus sieberi|E. sieberi]]''), [[banksia]]<ref name="Boland"/><!-- cites previous two sentences --> and such understory plants as burrawang (''[[Macrozamia communis]]'').<ref name=Fairley/> It is a component tree of wetland forest in [[Booderee National Park]] alongside blackbutt, red bloodwood, grey ironbark (''[[Eucalyptus paniculata]]''), scribbly gum (''[[Eucalyptus sclerophylla|E. sclerophylla]]''), old man banksia (''[[Banksia serrata]]''), coast banksia (''[[Banksia integrifolia|B. integrifolia]]'') and snow-in-summer (''[[Melaleuca linariifolia]]''), with understory plants such as jointed twig-rush (''[[Baumea articulata]]''), tall spike-rush (''[[Eleocharis sphacelata]]''), prickly tea-tree (''[[Leptospermum juniperinum]]''), and zig-zag bog-rush (''[[Schoenus brevifolius]]'').<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Roe, John H.|author2=Georges, Arthur|year=2007|title=Heterogeneous wetland complexes, buffer zones, and travel corridors: Landscape management for freshwater reptiles|journal=Biological Conservation|volume=135|pages=67–76|url=http://wildlifegenomics.biomatix.org/storage/app/uploads/public/58a/0f6/c2e/58a0f6c2e642d933195795.pdf |doi=10.1016/j.biocon.2006.09.019}}</ref>

==Ecology==
''Eucalyptus botryoides'' [[Fire regime|regenerates after bushfire]] by resprouting from epicormic buds and its woody lignotuber. Plants have been dated at 600 years of age.<ref name=bm871/> It also drops branches,<ref name=Ben98/> and these have been known to grow roots. The wet environment and water-absorbing qualities of the thick, fibrous bark facilitate this.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Lacey | first1 = C. J. | last2 = Gillison | first2 = A. N. | last3 = Whitecross | first3 = M. I. | doi = 10.1071/BT9820147 | title = Root Formation by Stems of ''Eucalyptus botryoides'' Sm. In Natural Stands | journal = Australian Journal of Botany | volume = 30 | issue = 2 | pages = 147–59 | year = 1982 }}</ref>
The [[koala]] (''Phascalarctos cinereus'') eats the leaves, and ants consume the nectar. The species is highly susceptible to psyllids.<ref name=Ben98/>

==Uses==
The heartwood of this species is durable and heavy (about 765–985 kg/m<sup>3</sup>), and resembles that of ''E. saligna'' and ''E. grandis''. It is used for flooring and panelling.<ref name="Boland"/>
